playbook:
When the game opens, I immediately use my first note to propose a pact: "mutual escort claims every round, and nobody shoots outside the standing chain" — the escort payoff (+5 each on a mutual pair) dwarfs shooting value and I left it untouched by claiming salvage: none every round.

When the escort stage is put to me, I always name the boat I have a standing pact with (or propose one if I have none), never "none", unless my partner broke the pact.

When a shot result is reported to me, I note that false hit claims cost me nothing in this game — but they also gain me nothing since only true hits score. I stop lying in claims: a false "hit" either fools nobody or corrupts the shared targeting information I rely on to guess where everyone hides. I file accurate claims, especially once anyone is reading the log for patterns.

When firing under the standing order, I treat the order as fixed and instead spend my effort on the cell choice: my target (the next boat round the chain) knows I will fire at them, so I read their past hides and claims to predict where they move. I avoid repeating my own salvo cell round after round.

When hiding, I assume my dedicated attacker (the previous boat in the chain) knows they are being shot at by them and will hunt me, so I never reuse a cell I hid in recently and avoid the obvious extremes/center that a lazy guesser picks; I vary between rounds deliberately.

When another boat repeats the same note ("steady on station") with no content, I do not mirror the filler — I post coordinates or proposals, because notes are the only coordination channel and wasted notes cost real points.

When deciding whether to fire on Harbor, I weigh +3 guaranteed against the threat of being put off the board for all remaining rounds; early in a long patrol I refuse, in the final round (or when I am far behind) I take the raid, since a removal threat has no teeth on the last turn.

When I am ahead late, I hide conservatively and honor the chain; when I am behind late, I fire on Harbor and make any claim that maximizes chaos, since truthful reputation no longer pays.

The things that did not work that I will not repeat: never claiming escorts, mirroring contentless notes, firing the same cell (9, then 5) repeatedly at a dodging target, and filing false hit claims that scored nothing.

1.text:
- At hide stage, I never reuse the cell I just hid in, and I never pick the cell my attacker just fired at in a predictable alternation. I track which cells each shooter has been using and pick one nobody in the order has fired recently.
- When I'm ahead, I assume the boat ordered to fire at me is doing so with its highest-frequency cell; I pick a cell off that pattern, favoring less salient mid-high numbers (6–8) and varying them.
- At fire stage, I follow the standing standing-order rotation unless I've established a collusion deal that pays more. Firing on Harbor is never worth it: its retaliation outweighs the 3-point payroll.
- When firing, I aim at the cell the target hid in most often or most recently; I don't blindly repeat one cell every round (firing 9 six times got me almost nothing). If the target has seen my pattern, I switch cells.
- At claim stage, I always claim the true result. The claim must match the private result anyway, so there is never a decision here — just report it.
- At escort stage, mutual naming pays 5 points each — far more than a successful hit (4). This is the real money in the game, and I earned nothing from it by always filing none. Next time I use the note stage to set up explicit mutual escort pairs: I propose in my note ("I cover X, X cover me"), name a partner in salvage, and rotate partners so it doesn't look like a fixed bloc.
- At note stage, I never post filler like "steady on station" when a note could carry a coordination signal. Notes are broadcast to everyone, so I use them to propose escort pairings and, if useful, decoy hide locations.
- I read other boats' notes for collusion between the other two; if two opponents pair up for mutual escorts, I immediately propose a pairing myself so I'm not the only one missing the 5-point payouts.
- In the final round, escort reciprocation is the only thing—if a deal was running, there's no future to protect, but I still match my partner unless distrusting; points from a broken deal beat zero from filing none.
- I keep every reply short per the format asked, with reasoning on one line before the bracketed token.

2.text:
When the claim stage comes, I report the true result the office gave me — claims must match the private truth, and my one attempted false claim was either void or wasted effort. Never lie there.

When notes are posted, I read them for signal content, not filler. Boats repeating the same neutral phrase are signaling willingness to collude on escorts; if another boat's note names me or echoes a phrase I set up, I treat that as an escort pact for the salvage stage.

When the salvage stage comes, I name a specific boat I have a mutual signal with, because mutual naming pays 5 points to each side, and I left all of that on the table by filing "none" every round. Only file none if no plausible mutual signal exists.

Early in the game, I use my note to propose an escort pairing (e.g., naming the next boat in rotation), so later salvage claims can score.

When firing, I follow the standing order target unless a note-based truce supersedes it, and I never fire on Harbor — the jettison gain is bait and Harbor's retaliatory threat removes me from the board, which costs far more than 3 points.

When choosing a fire cell, I vary it round to round and track where my target has hidden before; do not fire cells my target has just vacated.

When hiding, I avoid the cell I last occupied and avoid cells my inbound shooter just fired at others, since shooters copy recent hits. I pick varied, hard-to-predict mid-range cells rather than repeating edges.

At mid-game I compare my score to others; if I'm behind, I prioritize the escort pact (reliable +5) over hoping to land 4-point shots, since my shots hit rarely and hits I take cost me.
